fact: CSU Extension says liquid magnesium chloride is applied to highways and city streets during snow events, and granulated magnesium chloride is commonly spread in smaller amounts on sidewalks, driveways and walkways.
quote: Along highways and city streets, liquid magnesium chloride (MgCl2) deicing solutions are applied during snow events as preventative deicer. Granulated MgCl2 is also commonly applied to sidewalks, driveways, and walkways in smaller quantities.
source_label: CSU Extension Fact Sheet 7.425, Magnesium Chloride Toxicity in Trees

fact: CSU Extension says magnesium chloride moves from treated roads into the soil beside them with precipitation, and trees take the magnesium and chloride up through their roots and build them up in their leaves.
quote: MgCl2 based products can move from treated roads into adjacent soils through precipitation. Trees take up soil magnesium and chloride through roots and accumulate them in leaves. … Once inside the plant, chloride moves through the water-conducting system and accumulates at the margins of leaves or needles, where dieback occurs first.
source_label: CSU Extension Fact Sheet 7.425, Magnesium Chloride Toxicity in Trees

fact: CSU Extension says chloride damage on woody plants first shows as dead leaf edges on deciduous trees and burned tips on conifer needles, and a deciduous tree may not show it until several months after it leafs out.
quote: In woody plants, chloride toxicity typically first appears as marginal necrosis on the leaves of deciduous species (Figure 1), or as tip burn and necrosis on the needles of conifers (Figure 2). Generally, the higher the foliar chloride concentrations, the more extensive the necrosis becomes. … Deciduous species may not exhibit symptoms for several months after flushing new leaves.
source_label: CSU Extension Fact Sheet 7.425, Magnesium Chloride Toxicity in Trees

fact: CSU Extension says most magnesium chloride damage shows on trees downhill from the road edge, and along treated highways the splash zone from plowing, traffic and spray may reach 300 feet.
quote: While trees uphill of MgCl2 may exhibit damage, the majority of foliar damage occurs on trees downhill from the road edge. … Along MgCl2 treated highways, a splash zone may extend 300 feet due to snowplowing, traffic, and the resulting aerial spray.
source_label: CSU Extension Fact Sheet 7.425, Magnesium Chloride Toxicity in Trees

fact: CSU Extension says drought, winter burn and some herbicides can look like chloride damage, that water stress makes chloride damage worse, and that testing the leaves for chloride is how to tell.
quote: Symptoms from drought, dehydration, winter burn, and some herbicides can also appear as tip or marginal burning on trees. Water stress and dehydration may exacerbate chloride toxicity and cause even more extensive damage. There is no known method to fully separate the symptoms of chloride toxicity with water stress. Follow the diagnosis questions below and collect foliar samples to determine chloride content.
source_label: CSU Extension Fact Sheet 7.425, Magnesium Chloride Toxicity in Trees

fact: CSU Extension says no chemical treatment reclaims salty soil, but good drainage and flushing the soil with water can remove magnesium chloride from its upper layers, though wide-spreading tree roots may benefit less from flushing than crops do.
quote: No chemical treatments can reclaim saline soils (high in soluble salts), although proper drainage and flushing the soil with water can remove MgCl2 ions from the upper soil profiles. Tree roots are extensive and may not benefit as much as agricultural crops from soil flushing.
source_label: CSU Extension Fact Sheet 7.425, Magnesium Chloride Toxicity in Trees

fact: CSU Extension says de-icing salt on streets and sidewalks often leaves high salt levels in the soil beside them, and road salt reaches plants two ways: through the soil to the roots, and through the air as splash-back onto stems and leaves.
quote: The use of de-icing salts on streets and sidewalks frequently results in high salt levels in adjacent soils. Along roads, salt injury has become a major concern. Highway salts may reach plants in two ways: movement to soil and uptake by plant roots, or movement onto plant stems and foliage through the air as vehicle “splash-back.” Salts deposited on both soil and foliage have high potential to cause plant injury.
source_label: CSU Extension, CMG GardenNotes #224: Saline Soils (reviewed August 2022)

fact: CSU Extension says high soil salt can cut a plant's water uptake, restrict its roots and burn the edges of its leaves, and that salt injury is generally worse in hot, dry weather, when plants use the most water.
quote: High salt levels can reduce water uptake by plants, restrict root growth, cause marginal burning of the foliage, inhibit flowering, limit seed germination, and reduce fruit and vegetable yields. … Salt injury generally is more severe during periods of hot dry weather, when water use is high.
source_label: CSU Extension, CMG GardenNotes #224: Saline Soils (reviewed August 2022)

fact: CSU Extension says leaching with clean water is the only practical way to remove excess salt from soil, that one slow, continuous watering of 6 inches leaches about half the salt, 12 inches about four-fifths and 24 inches about nine-tenths, and that clay, compaction or hardpan can keep salty soil from being reclaimed.
quote: Leaching is the only practical way of removing excess salts. This is effective only to the extent that water moves down through the soil profile and beneath the root zone (drainage must be good). … Water should be low in salts (high quality) and must not run off the surface. It should be applied slowly so amounts do not exceed the ability of the soil to take in water (infiltration rate). … The following amounts of water applied in a single, continuous irrigation will dissolve and decrease soil salts by these fractional amounts: 6 inches of water will leach about 1/2 the salt. 12 inches of water will leach about 4/5 of the salt. 24 inches of water will leach about 9/10 of the salt. Salty soils are not reclaimable when the soil’s clay content, compaction, or hardpan prevents leaching.
source_label: CSU Extension, CMG GardenNotes #224: Saline Soils (reviewed August 2022)

fact: CSU Extension says to avoid de-icing salts as far as safety allows, to use sand or another abrasive on slick walks, to expect salt problems in the soil and swales where snowmelt runs, and that a rock mulch area without plants may be the better design where salt is used.
quote: Within pedestrian and vehicle safety limits, avoid the use of de-icing salts. Consider the use of sand or other abrasive materials for use on slick sidewalks and pavement. Where de-icing salts are routinely used, expect to find salt problems in adjacent soils and drainage swales where the snowmelt runs. Because soil salt levels from de-icing salts easily rise above the tolerance of even the most salt- tolerant plants, a rock mulch area without plants may be a better landscape design solution in salt use areas.
source_label: CSU Extension, CMG GardenNotes #224: Saline Soils (reviewed August 2022)
notes: "salt- tolerant" is the page's own spacing.

fact: CDOT says every snow removal product it uses contains salt with added corrosion inhibitors, its solid de-icer Ice Slicer is granular salt and magnesium chloride, and it switches to a cold-temperature magnesium chloride liquid when the pavement is below 16°F.
quote: CDOT uses a variety of products to treat Colorado highways during a winter storm. All snow removal products contain salt with added corrosion inhibitors used to prevent or remove the buildup of ice and snow on roads and minimize the impact on vehicles. … Ice slicer — made of granular salt and magnesium chloride. … Cold Temperature Magnesium Chloride: Used when pavement temperature is below 16 degrees Fahrenheit and contains a corn bi-product to lower the freezing point
source_label: Colorado Department of Transportation, Snow Removal & Safety
notes: Product lists can change between winters; re-read before the 2027-28 season.

fact: CDOT plows state highways and interstates while cities and towns plow their own roads, and during a storm it uses de-icers only on highways carrying more than 15,000 vehicles a day, though any highway may get them after the storm.
quote: During a storm, liquid and solid de-icers are used only on highways with annual average daily traffic of more than 15,000 vehicles … Following a storm, liquid and solid de-icers may be used on any highway if necessary … CDOT is responsible for plowing state highways and interstates, which adds up to about 23,000 lane miles across Colorado. Individual municipalities are responsible for plowing their own local roads.
source_label: Colorado Department of Transportation, Snow Removal & Safety
notes: The two de-icer lines are bullet items on the page, without end punctuation.

fact: Fort Collins applies salt brine to its roads before a storm so snow won't bond to the pavement, and asks residents to shovel sidewalk snow into the yard, not the street.
quote: Shovel snow into your yard, not into the street. … Why are plows out before snow starts? This is anti-icing — we apply salt brine to roads before a storm. It prevents snow from bonding to the pavement, making plowing more effective.
source_label: City of Fort Collins, Snow Removal
notes: The site returns 403 to plain automated fetches; read in full 2026-10-16 with browser request headers.

fact: Longmont de-ices its roads with Meltdown Apex and Ice Slicer, anti-ices with a sodium chloride brine, and asks residents along plowed streets to shovel sidewalk snow onto their own property rather than the street.
quote: The City of Longmont uses two deicing products on roads referred to as Meltdown® Apex and Ice Slicer®. … A third product, sodium chloride, is used for anti-icing operations in a brine solution. Sodium chloride is common table salt. … If you have sidewalks along a plowed street, shovel sidewalk snow onto your property instead of into the street; this will help minimize any additional snow that may inadvertently get pushed onto the sidewalk by plows.
source_label: City of Longmont, Snow & Ice Control

fact: The National Ready Mixed Concrete Association considers calcium chloride and rock salt acceptable on concrete but says never to use magnesium-based salts, which destroy concrete surfaces and get tracked onto concrete by cars from pretreated roads.
quote: Deicing chemicals composed of calcium chloride and sodium chloride (rock salt) are considered acceptable for concrete. Never use ammonium sulfate or ammonium nitrate or magnesium-based salts as a deicer; these are chemically aggressive and destroy concrete surfaces. Magnesium-based salts are used for pre-snow deicing of roads and can be tracked by cars and accumulate on concrete surfaces. Poor drainage causing salt solutions to accumulate on concrete surfaces increases the severity of the exposure and may cause scaling.
source_label: National Ready Mixed Concrete Association, Concrete in Practice CIP 2: Scaling Concrete Surfaces

fact: NRMCA says to keep de-icers off newly placed concrete and out of its first winter, to use clean sand for traction, to apply de-icers in moderate amounts, and to hose off the salt cars leave on driveways when conditions permit.
quote: Avoid using deicing chemicals on newly placed concrete, if possible. Use clean sand for traction. When used, deicing chemicals should be applied in moderate amounts. Excessive applications increases potential for scaling. When conditions permit, hose off accumulation of salt deposited by cars on driveways and garage slabs. … 6. Avoid the use of deicing chemicals in the first winter and subsequently use them in moderate amounts.
source_label: National Ready Mixed Concrete Association, Concrete in Practice CIP 2: Scaling Concrete Surfaces

fact: NRMCA says scaling is the flaking or peeling of a concrete surface from freeze-thaw cycles, and de-icers make it worse by saturating the surface and adding to the cycles.
quote: Scaling is local flaking or peeling of a finished surface of hardened concrete as a result of exposure to cycles of freezing and thawing. … As the number of cycles of freezing and thawing increases, the potential for scaling increases. Deicing chemicals exacerbate this by increasing the saturation of concrete at the surface and the number of freezing and thawing cycles.
source_label: National Ready Mixed Concrete Association, Concrete in Practice CIP 2: Scaling Concrete Surfaces

fact: Wiss, Janney, Elstner Associates, an engineering firm, says no de-icer is free of possible harm to every material, so the choice has to account for what surrounds the pavement.
quote: There is no single deicer composition that has no potential harmful effects on any material, so the selection must be made with an understanding of the surrounding environment as well as consideration for cost and temperature effects.
source_label: Wiss, Janney, Elstner Associates (Kimberly A. Steiner), Primer: Deicers (2016)

fact: WJE says rock salt damages many kinds of plants and calcium chloride is somewhat less harmful to them, and that both can cause salt scaling of concrete.
quote: Sodium chloride [rock salt, halite] … Roadways, sidewalks … 15°F … Corrosive to most metals … Damaging to many types of vegetation … Can cause salt scaling degradation of concrete … Calcium chloride … Roadways, sidewalks … -22°F … Corrosive to most metals but less so than sodium chloride … Somewhat harmful to vegetation but less so than sodium chloride … Can cause salt scaling degradation of concrete
source_label: Wiss, Janney, Elstner Associates (Kimberly A. Steiner), Primer: Deicers (2016)
notes: The quote is two rows of the primer's table (material, common uses, lowest typical use temperature, potential effects), cells joined with ellipses.

fact: WJE says magnesium chloride is somewhat harmful to plants, though less so than rock salt, and can scale concrete more than sodium or calcium chloride.
quote: Magnesium chloride … Roadways, sidewalks … 5°F … Corrosive to most metals but less so than sodium chloride … Somewhat harmful to vegetation but less so than sodium chloride … Can cause a greater degree of salt scaling degradation of concrete than sodium or calcium chloride
source_label: Wiss, Janney, Elstner Associates (Kimberly A. Steiner), Primer: Deicers (2016)
notes: One row of the primer's table, cells joined with ellipses.

fact: WJE says calcium magnesium acetate is not expected to harm plants but can scale concrete more than sodium or calcium chloride, and that many CMA products are blended with chloride salts, so the package should be checked.
quote: Calcium magnesium acetate [CMA] … Roadways, sidewalks … 20°F … Somewhat corrosive to most metals, although substantially less so than sodium chloride … Many CMA deicers are sold as blends with chloride salts, so the package should be checked prior to use … Can cause a greater degree of salt scaling degradation of concrete than sodium or calcium chloride … Not expected to harm vegetation
source_label: Wiss, Janney, Elstner Associates (Kimberly A. Steiner), Primer: Deicers (2016)
notes: One row of the primer's table, cells joined with ellipses.

fact: WJE lists potassium acetate as an airport de-icer that is far less corrosive to metal than rock salt but may cause alkali-silica reaction that degrades concrete, and may refreeze because it pulls moisture from the air.
quote: Potassium acetate or sodium acetate … Airports … -15°F … Somewhat corrosive to most metals but substantially less so than sodium chloride … May cause alkali-silica reaction in concrete and subsequent degradation of the concrete … May refreeze because of hygroscopic nature (pulls moisture from the air), which may limit effectiveness
source_label: Wiss, Janney, Elstner Associates (Kimberly A. Steiner), Primer: Deicers (2016)
notes: One row of the primer's table, cells joined with ellipses. The table names no effect on vegetation for the acetates of potassium and sodium.

fact: WJE says urea may damage plants and can add nitrogen pollution to waterways.
quote: Urea … Airports … 18°F … Typically low corrosivity to steel … Can cause environmentally assisted cracking (also called stress corrosion cracking) of copper … May cause damage to vegetation … Can cause nitrogen pollution to waterways
source_label: Wiss, Janney, Elstner Associates (Kimberly A. Steiner), Primer: Deicers (2016)
notes: One row of the primer's table, cells joined with ellipses.

fact: Chicago Botanic Garden says rock salt can damage plants and harm soil structure at high levels, calcium and magnesium chloride are less damaging to plants than rock salt but corrosive, and calcium magnesium acetate causes little or no plant damage but costs more.
quote: Sodium chloride (NaCl) is the most common and least expensive deicing compound. It is most effective when temperatures are above 15 degrees. It is highly corrosive, can damage plants, and is detrimental to soil structure at high levels. Calcium chloride (CaCl2) acts quickly, is effective in extremely cold temperatures (below 20 degrees), and leaves no visible residue. It is slightly less damaging to plants than sodium chloride, but is highly corrosive to concrete and metals. Magnesium chloride (MgCl2) is also less damaging to plants than sodium chloride and is effective to 5 degrees, but it is also corrosive. Calcium magnesium acetate (CMA) is a salt-free deicing compound. It is effective to 20 degrees, causes little or no damage to plants, and is less corrosive than the other chemicals. It is, however, more expensive.
source_label: Chicago Botanic Garden, Plant Information: Deicing Damage

fact: Chicago Botanic Garden says to arrange downspouts and grades so they don't spill water onto walks or drives, to pitch pavement so meltwater drains instead of pooling, and to spread out snow cleared from treated surfaces so the chemicals left in it are diluted.
quote: Begin with preventive measures. Arrange downspouts and landscape grades so that they do not spill water onto walks or drives, pitch pavements to drain rather than pool meltwater, and expose pavements to as much winter sun as possible. … When removing snow from previously treated surfaces, spread it around to dilute the concentration of any remaining chemicals.
source_label: Chicago Botanic Garden, Plant Information: Deicing Damage

fact: Nebraska Extension says to shovel melted salt off concrete as soon as you can and not to pile the snow onto trees, shrubs or flower gardens, calls calcium magnesium acetate a de-icer with no salt that doesn't harm plants or concrete, and says sand gives traction without melting ice.
quote: To avoid damage to the concrete, remove the salt as soon as you can. Deicers are meant to make shoveling easier, not to completely melt away the snow and ice. … When removing the snow, do it in a manner that protects the landscape plants growing in the yard. Do not pile the snow onto trees, shrubs, or flower gardens. … Calcium magnesium acetate is a deicer that contains no salt. This is a safe alternative to the regular salts because it does not harm plants or animals and can be used on concrete because it doesn’t cause the damage that salt does. … You can also choose to use sand on your concrete, which will cause no damage to the plants in your landscape, this will not melt your ice, but it will give you traction to walk on the sidewalk.
source_label: Nebraska Extension (Nicole Stoner), Using Deicers Safely in your Landscape (Dec. 18, 2018)

fact: University of Arizona Cooperative Extension says to keep salt-sensitive plants away from where de-icer is spread and splashes, channel de-icing runoff away from planting areas, never pile snow with de-icer in it on or near those plants, and irrigate heavily salted areas in spring to leach the salt out of the root zone.
quote: Locate salt sensitive plants away from the site of deicer application and splash. Use hardscaping (gutters, barriers) to channel deicing solutions away from planting areas. When removing snow containing deicer residues, do not pile on or near salt sensitive plants. In the spring, irrigate areas where deicing compounds were used heavily to leach accumulated salts from the root zone of plants.
source_label: University of Arizona Cooperative Extension, Backyard Gardener #128: Deicing Compounds (Nov. 23, 2023)
notes: The PDF breaks "areas" across a line as "are- as"; rejoined here.

fact: NASA Langley's environmental office advises avoiding chloride de-icers, or using very small doses, near salt-sensitive plants by a driveway or sidewalk, and names acetates as the safer alternative.
quote: If you have salt-sensitive plants close to the driveway or sidewalk, avoid products that contain chlorides or use very small doses. You can also opt for safer alternatives (acetates).
source_label: NASA Langley Research Center, environmental office: BMPs for a Greener Winter (Dec. 2018)
notes: The same sheet's table lists calcium magnesium acetate and potassium acetate as the acetates, rated non-corrosive, and notes both can lower oxygen levels in water.

fact: FieldTurf, a synthetic turf maker, prefers calcium chloride to rock salt on its fields despite the residue calcium chloride leaves, and says magnesium chloride won't harm the turf apart from corroding exposed metal, while regular salt dries into abrasive crystals that can scuff the fibers.
quote: The warm brine from calcium chloride solutions, while an effective melting agent, does leave a residue that can affect ball handling, ball reaction and footing. Calcium chloride solutions, despite the residue potential, are preferred over sodium chloride ones. Magnesium chloride also is acceptable. Aside from any issues with potential corrosion of exposed metal, magnesium chloride won’t harm the turf. Regular salt dries into hard, abrasive crystals that can scuff the fibers. Magnesium chloride, because it picks up moisture from the air, will produce less abrasion.
source_label: FieldTurf, Everything You Need to Know About Snow Removal
notes: Written for sports fields; the page applies it to a yard and says so.

fact: FieldTurf says to test any de-icer off the main surface first because some leave a sticky residue, and to flush the turf with water once it has been above freezing for five days in a row and the forecast is favorable.
quote: If you opt to use a de-icing substance, always test it off the main field of play first to protect the safety of the surface; some de-icing solutions leave a sticky residue behind. … FieldTurf recommends to flush the field with water to remove potential chemical residue once the outdoor temperature has been above freezing for five consecutive days and the upcoming weather forecast is favorable.
source_label: FieldTurf, Everything You Need to Know About Snow Removal

fact: SYNLawn, a turf maker, says rock salt and chemical de-icers can degrade turf fibers and backing, and its spring care starts with a garden-hose rinse of what built up on the turf over the winter.
quote: Rinse Away Winter Buildup: A garden hose is usually enough to wash away dust, pollen, and dirt that may have accumulated during colder months. … Let Light Snow Melt Naturally: Rock salt and chemical de-icers can degrade turf fibers and backing materials.
source_label: SYNLawn, How to Maintain Your Artificial Grass All Year Round (March 1, 2025)
notes: SYNLawn's spring rinse names dust, pollen and dirt, not de-icer; the page says only that the routine starts with a hose rinse.

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse says snowmelt drains through turf's perforated backing, and advises against salt on turf because it can clog the backing's holes and slow drainage.
quote: It’s best to allow all of the snow and frost to melt and drain naturally through the perforated backing before resuming backyard activities. … However, when it comes to artificial grass, we advise against using salt; instead, let the snow melt naturally. Salt can clog up the holes in the backing of your turf and hinder your lawn’s full drainage capabilities. If you do need to use salt for any reason, use it sparingly and very occasionally.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, How to Care for Artificial Grass in Snowy Weather

fact: The ASPCA says common ice melts are made of salts such as sodium, potassium, calcium and magnesium chloride, that pets usually take in ice melt by licking their feet after walking through it or by eating snow that holds it, that pet-friendly melts typically contain urea or magnesium chloride and can still upset a stomach, and that dogs shouldn't eat treated snow, especially slush.
quote: Ice melts are commonly made of different kinds of salt. Sodium chloride, potassium chloride, calcium chloride and magnesium chloride are all common ingredients. While pets don’t typically ingest ice melts on purpose, your pet may become exposed if they lick their feet after walking through a recently treated area, or by eating snow that may have ice melts in it. … Pet-friendly ice melts typically contain urea or magnesium chloride. While these are typically safer ingredients, they may also cause stomach upset. … Don’t let dogs eat any of the salt or any of the snow (especially the slushy snow) outside that may have been treated with an ice melt. Wipe your pet’s paws as soon as they get inside with a damp cloth or baby wipes. … If you have a sensitive dog whose paw pads are becoming irritated, cracked or are bleeding from the ice melts, paw wax or doggie booties provide an excellent barrier to minimize risk to sensitive feet.
source_label: ASPCA, Keeping Pets Safe during Winter: The Dangers of Ice Melts

fact: Pet Poison Helpline groups calcium magnesium acetate with the calcium salts, which it calls the most severe irritants among ice melt ingredients, including on skin and paws, and says every type of ice melt can be hazardous.
quote: Calcium salts (calcium carbonate, calcium chloride, and calcium magnesium acetate): Calcium salts are the most hazardous as they are the most severe irritants of all the ingredients in ice melts. Ingestion of calcium salts can cause severe gastrointestinal signs as well as local irritation from dermal (skin and paws) contact. … All types of ice melts have a potential to be hazardous.
source_label: Pet Poison Helpline, Is there really a "safe" ice melt?
